title: Ramadan: the last ten
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ tightened his belt and woke his family in the last ten (Bukhari)

cards: In everyday English, tightening your belt means cutting back. Spending less. Getting by.
In a report from 'A'ishah in Sahih al-Bukhari, it means almost the opposite. She describes what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, did when the last ten nights of Ramadan began.
In paraphrase: he tightened his waist-wrapper, he brought his nights to life, and he woke his family. Not cutting back. Gearing up.
The month was nearly over, and instead of coasting toward the finish, he went harder.

teach.b: Take her three phrases one at a time. He tightened his waist-wrapper: scholars read this two ways. Some say it means serious effort, the way a worker cinches a belt before lifting.
Others say he withdrew from his wives for those nights to give himself to worship. Some hold both. He brought his nights to life: he stayed awake in prayer instead of sleeping through them.
And he woke his family. He didn't keep the nights to himself. Why these nights?
The Qur'an names a night, the Night of Power, which you first met in year one. Surah al-Qadr says, in Pickthall's words: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months."
In another report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells people to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten. The report names no single night, so the way to find it is to show up for all of them.

teach.h: I'TIKAF: A RETREAT IN THE MOSQUE.
teach.b: Some go further and stay in the mosque. 'A'ishah says in al-Bukhari that he kept i'tikaf, a retreat in the mosque, in the last ten, and his wives kept it after him. And what to say if you find the night?
In al-Tirmidhi, 'A'ishah asks him exactly that.
He teaches her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon. Not for wealth. Not for a sign.
For pardon. So the last ten have a shape: effort, wakefulness, family, retreat, and at the center, one plain request.

how: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims add night prayer and look for the Night of Power in the odd nights, as hadiths in al-Bukhari describe; some stay in the mosque in a retreat called i'tikaf, and some repeat the short prayer for pardon the Prophet taught 'A'ishah, kept in al-Tirmidhi.

o: the fasting month, ending in ten nights of extra effort
the one night each year when the Qur'an is recited
a month that winds down gently into rest at its end

games.q: 'A'ishah asks the Prophet: if I knew which night is the Night of Power, what should I say? what does he teach her to ask for?
o: pardon, from Allah who loves to pardon.
a sign that the night has come.
games.why: in al-Tirmidhi he teaches her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon.

practice: Choose a night, in Ramadan if you keep it or any night this week if you don't, and picture the alarm going off in the dark, the house quiet, and you sitting up instead of rolling over.
What would you do with that hour: pray, read, sit in silence, write down what you're sorry for and thankful for? If you pray, you can ask for pardon, the way the Prophet taught 'A'ishah.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan. The month of fasting, which ends in ten nights of extra effort, with the Night of Power hidden somewhere among them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Night of Power, named in surah al-Qadr.

carryVoice: Your line: tighten the belt. Gearing up, not coasting, at the very end. Until tomorrow.
